newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian central bank backs govt's EMU forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Belgian central bank backs govt's EMU forecasts.

text.p: The National Bank of Belgium gave its first official backing on Friday to government efforts to reduce new borrowing in 1997 and qualify for a single European currency.

Releasing a raft of forecasts for the country's 1997 economic performance, the central bank said it expected the budget deficit to reach 2.9 percent of gross domestic product, in line with government forecasts despite slower-than-expected economic growth.

The bank said it saw growth of 2.0 percent in 1997, up from 1.4 percent in 1996 but below a 2.1 percent target fixed by the government last year and retained in a recent mini-budget designed to keep Belgium on course for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

The government said last month its budget was built upon a triple-safety margin: a deficit target below the three percent required for EMU membership; a "prudent" (below average) growth forecast and a 20 billion franc ($560 million) cushion to prevent any rise in interest rates from inflating the cost of servicing the country's huge debt.
The budget is vital for Belgium's bid to join EMU, membership of which is due to be decided upon the basis of economic indicators for this year.
The central bank effectively questioned the government's growth forecast but forecast lower inflation and unemployment.
Inflation should average 1.9 percent, down from 2.1 percent in 1996 and below a government forecast of 2.0 percent. The jobless rate should fall to 9.4 percent from 9.7 percent, the bank said.

The European Commission last November forecast Belgian growth for this year at 2.2 percent, inflation at 2.1 percent and unemployment at 9.9 percent. The Commission is due to release revised economic forecasts on April 23. ($ = 35.49 Belgian Francs)
